procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 29, 1964 of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 386 of 1963 (incorrectly referenced as 385 of 1963 in the text).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Judicial Magistrate overruled the appellant's objections.
2. Appellant took the matter in revision to the Sessions Judge of Mehsana.
3. Sessions Judge referred the matter to the High Court in Criminal Reference No. 14 of 1962.
4. High Court ordered that the complaint under s. 182, Indian Penal Code was bad but directed the trial court to decide whether the appellant was removable from his office save with the sanction of the Central Government.
5. Judicial Magistrate held that the appellant was not removable from his office save with the sanction of the Central Government and the complaint should be rejected.
6. The first respondent preferred a revision petition before the Sessions Judge of Mehsana who dismissed it.
7. The first respondent took the matter in revision to the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 385 of 1963.
8. The High Court held that the appellant being an officiating Class I Officer was removable by the Railway Board and no sanction of Central Government was necessary and directed that the case under ss. 166 and 167, Indian Penal Code should proceed against the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (original defendant) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the Gujarat High Court ruled against him, allowing the prosecution to proceed.

directions: The case under ss. 166 and 167, Indian Penal Code should proceed against the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government' within the meaning of s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, thereby necessitating the Central Government's sanction for his prosecution.

facts: The appellant was a public servant who, on the date of the complaint, held a substantive post as a Class II Officer but was officiating in a senior scale as a Class I Officer in the Western Railway.

He was prosecuted for offences under the Indian Penal Code, and he argued that the prosecution was invalid without the sanction of the Central Government, as required by s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The appellant was appointed to the officiating Class I position by the Railway Board.
law: Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code requires prior sanction from the Central Government to prosecute a public servant who is "not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government."
The legal principle of *qui facit per alium facit per se* (he who acts through another, acts himself) was considered.
The Railway Board Act, 1905, establishes the Railway Board as an entity separate from the Central Government, which derives its powers through delegation from the Central Government.
application: The Court first addressed the appellant's argument that the Railway Board was part and parcel of the Central Government. The Court rejected this, finding that the Railway Board Act, 1905, shows the Board is a separate body that exercises powers delegated to it by the Central Government, not in its own right as part of the government.

Since the appellant was appointed to the officiating Class I position by the Railway Board, the Court determined that the Railway Board was also the authority competent to remove him from that office.

The Court then rejected the appellant's second argument that even if the Railway Board was acting under delegated authority, the principle of *qui facit per alium facit per se* should apply, making the removal an act of the Central Government.

The Court held that once the Central Government delegates its power of appointment and removal to another authority (like the Railway Board), the public servant is no longer considered "not removable... except by... the Central Government" for the purposes of s. 197. To hold otherwise would improperly broaden the scope of the protection offered by the section.

The Court cited the precedent in *Afzalur Rahman v. The King Emperor*, which established that an officer removable by a subordinate authority under statutory rules is not covered by the protection of s. 197.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was not a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government.' Because the power to appoint and remove him from his officiating Class I post had been delegated to the Railway Board, a separate entity, the sanction of the Central Government under s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was not necessary for his prosecution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies when the Central Government delegates its power of removal, meaning the public servant is still deemed removable only by the Central Government for the purposes of s. 197 CrPC.

facts: The Central Government delegated its power to appoint and remove certain public servants to the Railway Board.
The appellant was a public servant who was removable by the Railway Board under this delegated authority.
The appellant argued that the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' (he who acts through another, acts himself) should apply.

This would mean that even though the Railway Board performed the act of removal, it was legally an act of the Central Government, thus requiring the Central Government's sanction for prosecution under s. 197 CrPC.
law: The Court relied on the precedent set in 'Afzalur Rahman v. The King Emperor'.

In that case, it was held that a police officer who could be dismissed by a delegated authority (the Deputy Inspector-General of Police) was not a person "not removable from office except by or with the sanction of the Provincial Government" within the meaning of s. 197 CrPC.
The Court also considered the legislative policy behind s. 197, which is to limit the protection to a specific class of officers and not make it available to all public officers.
application: The Court reasoned that once the Central Government has delegated its power of removal to another authority, the public servant concerned is no longer treated as one who is "not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government" for the purposes of s. 197 CrPC.
The Court explicitly rejected the argument that the maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies in this context.

It warned that accepting this argument would ignore the legislative intent to limit the scope of s. 197 and would risk extending its protection to all public officers, which was not the purpose of the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' does not apply in this situation. Once the power of removal is delegated, the public servant is considered removable by the delegated authority (the Railway Board), not the Central Government, for the purposes of s. 197 CrPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a public servant 'not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Central Government' within the meaning of s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, thereby necessitating the Central Government's sanction for his prosecution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that he was a public servant who could not be removed from his office without the sanction of the Central Government.
Consequently, the complaint against him was not maintainable without the Central Government's sanction under s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
To support this, the appellant's counsel relied on the Note to Rule 1704 and Rule 1705 of the New Rules.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, inferred from the court's reasoning, was that the appellant was removable by an authority other than the Central Government (specifically, the Railway Board).
The Note to Rule 1704, cited by the appellant, was irrelevant as it applied only to non-gazetted staff, whereas the appellant was a gazetted officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' applies when the Central Government delegates its power of removal, meaning the public servant is still deemed removable only by the Central Government for the purposes of s. 197 CrPC.
appellant_arguments: The appellant suggested that even if the Railway Board had the power to remove him, this power was merely delegated by the Central Government.

Therefore, based on the principle of 'qui facit per alium facit per se' (he who acts through another acts himself), the removal by the Railway Board should be treated as a removal by the Central Government, thus still requiring sanction under s. 197 CrPC.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, inferred from the court's rejection of the appellant's argument, is that the delegation of power to the Railway Board makes it the competent authority for removal.

The act of removal by the delegated authority (the Railway Board) is not considered an act by the Central Government for the purposes of s. 197 CrPC, and the legal maxim does not apply in this context.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If the Central Government delegates its power to appoint and remove a public servant to another authority, that public servant is not considered 'not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government' for the purposes of requiring sanction for prosecution under s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
obiter: The legislative policy is to limit the class of officers entitled to protection under s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, to avoid making it available to all public officers.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: If the Central Government has delegated its power to appoint and remove a public servant to another authority, such as the Railway Board, then for the purpose of s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, that public servant is no longer considered one who is 'not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government'. Consequently, the Central Government's sanction is not required for their prosecution.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if s. 197 CrPC applies, the court must identify the specific authority that has the power to remove the public servant from office. The test is not who holds the ultimate power, but who holds the delegated power of removal at the relevant time.
why_appellant_lost: The legal maxim 'qui facit per alium facit per se' does not apply in the context of s. 197 CrPC. The court held: 'even if it was acting under the powers delegated to it, the principle of the maxim qui facit per alium facit per se applies to the case... We do not think there is any substance in this argument.'

The act of delegation by the Central Government is legally determinative. The court reasoned: 'If once the Central Government has delegated its power to another authority with regard to appointment and removal of a public servant, then for the purpose of s. 197, Criminal Procedure Code the public servant concerned will not be treated to be a public servant "not removable from his office except by or with the sanction of the Central Government".'

The specific rules relied upon by the appellant were found to be inapplicable to his case, as he was a gazetted officer. 'The Note to r. 1704, and r. 1705, would not apply to the appellant, as the first applies only to non-gazetted officers.'
why_respondent_won: The court determined that the Railway Board, not the Central Government, was the competent authority to remove the appellant. 'It follows therefore that the appellant was removable from his office with the sanction of the Railway Board and the sanction of the President is not necessary for taking such action against the appellant.'

The court's reasoning was supported by the precedent set in 'Afzalur Rahman v. The King Emperor etc.', which held that a police officer dismissible by a delegated authority (the Deputy Inspector-General of Police) was not a person 'not removable from office except by or with the sanction of the Provincial Government' under s. 197 CrPC.
policy_considerations: The court sought to avoid an overly broad interpretation of s. 197 CrPC that would extend its protection to all public officers, contrary to legislative intent. Citing a previous case, it warned of 'the danger of our ignoring the policy of the Legislature in limiting the class of officers entitled to this protection and of making s. 197, Criminal Procedure Code available to all public officers.'
